opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Genie 2 was a really meaningful step, but I'd frame it as a step rather than a destination. With the original Genie, we showed that you could learn an action-controllable world from video alone, without any action labels, and that was exciting conceptually, but it was quite limited. It was 2D, low resolution, and the memory and consistency weren't really there for long horizons.

With Genie 2, the big jump was going to rich 3D environments. You can give it a single image prompt, which could be a real photo or a concept image from a text-to-image model, and it generates an interactive world that you can actually move through with keyboard and mouse actions. What surprised us was the emergent behavior: it models things like object interactions, character animation, physics such as water and smoke, lighting and reflections, and maybe most importantly some degree of memory. If you look away from part of the scene and then look back, it can often remember what was there. That kind of object permanence is something we didn't explicitly engineer in, and it came from scale and the right training setup.

That said, I try to be honest about the limitations. Consistency still degrades over longer horizons, typically tens of seconds up to about a minute. The fidelity isn't at a level where you'd mistake it for a real game engine, and the action space is still quite simple. So I'd assess it as strong evidence that the foundation world model approach works and scales, rather than proof that we've solved world modeling.

The reason we care so much is the bigger picture around embodied agents. One of the main bottlenecks for training generally capable agents is the lack of a sufficiently rich and diverse set of environments. If you can generate an essentially unlimited curriculum of novel, interactive worlds, that opens the door to training and evaluating agents in ways that weren't possible before. We did some early experiments putting our SIMA agent into Genie 2 worlds and having it follow instructions, and it was able to do things like navigate to a particular door. To me that was the most exciting part, because it closes the loop: the world model isn't just a cool demo, it's actually useful for agents.

So, a big step in breadth, in 3D, and in emergent capabilities, with clear next challenges around longer-horizon consistency, real-time interaction, and higher fidelity. That's very much the direction we've been pushing since.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think Genie 2 was a really significant step for us, and the way I'd frame it is in terms of what changed between Genie 1 and Genie 2. Genie 1 was trained on 2D platformer videos, so you could generate these little 2D worlds and control a character, which was a nice proof of concept that you could learn an action-controllable world model purely from unlabeled video. But it was quite limited: low resolution, 2D, and the horizons were short.

Genie 2 moved all of that into 3D. You take a single image, maybe a frame generated by Imagen, and the model produces a playable 3D environment that you can navigate with keyboard actions. And what surprised us, honestly, was how many emergent capabilities showed up just from scaling the data and the model. You get things like object interactions, physics that's roughly plausible, lighting and reflections, character animations, NPCs behaving in sensible ways. And crucially, some degree of memory: you could look away from part of the scene, turn back, and it was still there, at least for a while. None of that was explicitly built in.

So as a step toward a general world model, I'd say it validated the hypothesis that this is something you can learn from video at scale rather than needing to hand-engineer it. For us the big motivation is agents. If you want to train embodied agents and you're limited to the environments humans have coded up, you hit a ceiling very fast. A world model lets you generate an effectively unbounded curriculum of environments, and we did show early experiments where an agent could be dropped into Genie 2 worlds and follow instructions.

That said, I want to be honest about the limitations. Consistency over long horizons is still the hard problem. Genie 2 could hold things together for maybe up to a minute, but most of the time it was shorter, and the world would drift. Precise action control was also imperfect, so the gap between what you do and what happens isn't zero. And it's expensive, so you're not running it in real time at the quality you'd want. So I think of it less as the destination and more as the point where the research community, and we ourselves, became convinced this direction is real. The next steps are about consistency, controllability, and speed, and then actually closing the loop so agents learn inside these models in a meaningful way.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an exciting step, particularly in moving from generating a video to generating an environment you can interact with. For a world model, the important question is whether the world responds coherently to your actions. If you move somewhere, look away, and come back, does what you encounter still make sense?

That’s also what makes this direction interesting for training agents. You’d like to give an agent a broad range of environments where it can act, see consequences, and learn. But there’s a distinction between an environment that looks convincing and one that provides a reliable learning signal. So I’d assess Genie 2 as progress toward that goal, while still asking how consistent these worlds are over time and whether skills learned in them transfer to other environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about Genie 2 is the move toward worlds you can actually interact with. You’re not just generating a video and watching it unfold; you can take actions, and the model has to generate what happens as a consequence of those actions while keeping the environment coherent.

That makes it an interesting step toward training and evaluating agents. If we can generate a broad range of environments, we can ask whether an agent can handle situations it hasn’t encountered before, rather than becoming very good at a fixed set of tasks.

But I’d distinguish that progress from having a fully general simulator. Visual plausibility doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying physics or causal relationships are correct. Longer-term consistency and the diversity of interactions you can support are still important challenges. So I see Genie 2 as a promising step toward more general, actionable world models, with plenty left to solve.
